zh: 所有平方都是正数，固定序列的末项 r 时，起点越靠右平方和越小，所以每个末项最多对应一个起点；末项的平方不能超过 n，因此 r 只需枚举到 n 的整数平方根。
用滑动窗口：右端逐个加入 r 的平方，和超过 n 就从左端移除平方，直到不再超过；此时和恰好等于 n 就记下窗口。左端被移除后对更大的右端也只会更大，可以永久丢弃。最后按项数从多到少输出。
用整数平方根求出 R，左端从 1、窗口和从 0 开始；右端 r 从 1 到 R：加上 r²，当和大于 n 时减去左端平方并右移左端，若和等于 n 记录 (左端, r)。把记录按长度降序排序，先输出个数，再逐行输出长度和窗口里的所有整数；无解只输出 0。
en: All squares are positive, so for a fixed last term r, moving the start to the right strictly decreases the sum, which means each last term has at most one valid start. The last term's square cannot exceed n, so r only needs to go up to the integer square root of n.

Use a sliding window: add the square of each new right end, and while the sum exceeds n, remove squares from the left end. If the sum then equals n, record the window. A left end removed this way can only give larger sums for later right ends, so it can be dropped for good. Finally output the windows from most terms to fewest.

Compute R as the integer square root of n, and start with left = 1 and sum = 0. For r from 1 to R, add r squared; while the sum is greater than n, subtract the square of left and move left right; if the sum equals n, record (left, r). Sort the records by length in descending order, print their count, then one line per record with the length followed by all integers in the window. If there are none, print only 0.

explanationEn:
## Source and output conventions

fastprep/Trend Micro/trendmicro-find-sequences.md at the fixed commit e66f809f4c953bce129f68491726176615db6afc fully preserves 1≤n≤10^10 and the rule of finding all sequences of consecutive positive integers whose sum of squares equals n. The comparison symbols in the original HTML were swallowed by the catalog text parser, which made the range and the goal disappear; the original problem did not lack constraints. The output description first defines c as the number of terms in a sequence and then uses an uppercase C to require descending order; this site uniformly orders by number of terms, descending. A single-term sequence corresponds to m=0 in (p,…,p+m), and there is no extra requirement of at least two terms. The original has no public examples, so all public examples of this problem are explicitly added by this site.

The original interface returns an array of strings: the first item is the number of solutions, and each remaining item is the number of terms followed by all elements of the sequence. This site only serializes each string as one line; with no solution it outputs a single line 0, not None or -1, and it does not output the squared numbers. No new numeric limits are introduced, and no upstream code was executed.

## Approach

The last term r of a sequence satisfies r²≤n, so only 1≤r≤⌊√n⌋ need to be checked. Maintain the sum of squares of the consecutive window [l,r], adding r² on the right each time; while the sum is greater than n, remove l² from the left. If the current sum is exactly n, record the whole window. Sort all matching windows by length in descending order and output every integer of each window.

## Proof of correctness

All squared terms are strictly positive. For a fixed right end r, the window sum strictly decreases as the left end increases, so at most one left end makes the sum of squares equal n. When the algorithm removes an element from the left, the sum before removal is greater than n, so these left ends cannot produce a solution for the current right end; for any future, larger right end they only add positive amounts, so they can never produce a solution either, and discarding them permanently is safe.

After shrinking, the current left end is the smallest one not yet excluded. If the window sum equals n, it is the unique valid solution; if it is less than n, increasing the left end further only makes the sum smaller, so no solution is missed for this right end. Enumerating all possible right ends covers every non-empty sequence of consecutive positive integers, and every recorded window is checked by the actual sum-of-squares equality, so no solution is missed and no false solution is produced.

For a fixed length c, the sum of squares Σ(p+j)² strictly increases with the start p. Hence each length has at most one solution, and descending order by length gives the unique required order, with no need for a tie rule.

## Complexity and full range

Let R=⌊√n⌋, K be the number of solutions, and L be the total number of terms in all output sequences. The left and right pointers each move at most R times, so the time is O(R+K log K+L), and the space including the stored output is O(K+L). In this problem R≤100000. The sum of the first 3106 squares starting from 1 does not exceed 10^10, while the sum of the first 3107 squares exceeds it, so any solution has at most 3106 terms. Each length has at most one solution, so K≤3106 and L≤3106×3107/2=4825171, and the full output fits within a 64 MiB budget. Use an integer square root and 64-bit integers to avoid floating-point boundary issues; the running window sum is at most 2n≤2×10^10, which a 64-bit signed integer holds easily.

## Independent verification

The oracle enumerates by length c and then binary searches the start p over integers using the closed form c·p²+c(c−1)·p+c(c−1)(2c−1)/6. It does not slide a window and does not reuse the reference program. 163 unique inputs were cross-checked against real subprocesses. The official stress cases keep n=10^10, values next to the upper bound, 99999², the sum of squares of length 3106 and its neighbors, and include inputs with multiple solutions and with none. Every output integer is compared in full, not just the number of solutions. Two wrong programs, one missing single-term sequences and one reversing the length order, must exit normally and be rejected by the official cases.
